newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Croatian leader takes election to Bosnian Croats.
newsitem.headline: Croatian leader takes election to Bosnian Croats.

text.p: Croatian President Franjo Tudjman took his country's election campaign into Croat-held Bosnia on Saturday, visiting an enclave of loyal supporters to boost his struggling party.

In a one-day trip to postwar Bosnia's Herzegovina region controlled by Croat separatists backed by Tudjman, he praised local inhabitants for their support of Croatia's independence war in 1991 and their toughness in war and peace.

"You Bosnian Croats in many ways set examples for all Croatians," he said in a speech after ceremonially opening an aluminium plant in the city of Mostar, which is divided between Croats and Moslems aligned with Bosnia's central government.
Tudjman has reached back to wartime Croatian patriotic themes in a bid to shore up his HDZ party's campaign for April 13 municipal elections to be held across Croatia.

The HDZ's popular appeal has seriously declined in the past two years due to authoritarian behaviour and reputed corruption. Centrist opposition party coalitions could defeat the HDZ in a number of major towns next month, polls show.

Tudjman did not mention an incident in which European Union officials walked out of the factory inauguration ceremony over insults in a speech by plant director Mijo Brajkovic, the rightist former mayor of west Mostar.
Brajkovic blasted the EU, especially postwar Mostar's ex-transitional administrator Hans Koschnick, for the factory's decay because it did not provide reconstruction funds.
Tudjman tried to look energetic but his voice cracked often and he appeared wizened from illness, diagnosed by American physicians last November as apparently terminal stomach cancer.

Diplomats said then that Tudjman, 74, did not have long to live. But an international group of doctors who later treated and examined him at home declared he had recovered enough to exercise his duties for the forseeable future.
Bosnian Croats wield significant influence in Tudjman's government and helped finance his climb to power in 1990. Many have Croatian citizenship and can vote in Croatian elections.
But they are resented by many Croatians for their favoured position and ultra-nationalist, anti-European tendencies.
Later in the day, Tudjman moved on to the nearby Roman Catholic shrine town of Medjugorje near the Croatian border where he was welcomed by ecstatic Croat crowds.
In a speech in front of the central church there, he again dwelled on the past of Croatia's bloody fight for statehood.
"Susak and many people from (Croat) Herzegovina and Bosnia were by our side in defending Croatia," he said, inviting them to vote for "people who knew how to create what we have now".

"Herzegovina is one of the pillars of Croatdom as a whole," he said in a remark resembling others which have prompted Bosnian Moslem leaders to accuse Croatia of trampling on Bosnia's territorial sovereignty.
Under Western pressure, Croatian police last month arrested two top Bosnian Croat mobsters who orchestrated evictions of Moslems from their homes in Croat-controlled West Mostar.
Diplomats saw the crackdown then as a bid by Tudjman to jettison Mostar hardliners damaging the HDZ's image. His move was unpopular among Bosnian Croats.
His visit on Saturday might have been partly intended to win back their favour.
